speechtext:
I am not suggesting that. I am suggesting that North Sydney and Halifax should get the same kind of law, as it applies to vessels coming in and making purchases, as Newfoundland is getting at the present time. Of course I realize that the Department of Fisheries is rather supernumerary in the matter of Newfoundland fisheries, when consideration is given to the fisheries commission in Newfoundland, the powers they have, and the restrictions with regard to becoming a member of the fisheries commission. If I were the minister I imagine I would figure that, with regard to Newfoundland, I was merely attached for rations and discipline, when consideration is given to the scope of that commission which has been perpetuated for ten years under the terms of confederation. But that is another argument altogether and I am not going to enter into it. In fact, it is none of my business. We shall let the premier of Newfoundland, Mr. Smallwood, work this thing out.
The two things on which I wish the minister to comment are, first, the fishing bounty, and what is going to be done about it; and second, how are we going to enforce the regulations with regard to these foreign ships making purchases in the ports that I have mentioned?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, probably I should answer some of these questions before I get too far behind. First I should like to reply to a question that was asked of me on the orders of the day yesterday by the hon. member for Cumberland. The question was with regard to extension of the lobster season in that area. We find that this year to date there has been a slightly lower catch of lobsters than there was last year, although not a great deal. We have therefore not fully made up our minds yet just what we will do. But if there is any extension-and it is likely that there will be some-it will apply to the whole of that district, not just to one part of it. Our announcement will be made shortly.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Can the minister state when the announcement will be made?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
It will be made by the first of next week at the latest, but probably this week.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo made an extremely interesting speech. He dealt with two important problems, one of which is the danger to stocks from the use of draggers. I think probably there has now been sufficient experience in the use of draggers to determine whether or not there is a depletion of the stock in the areas where draggers are being used. That question has to be constantly examined and reports made. The information we have to date is that the use of draggers has not in general diminished the supply, although if there is constant use of draggers in a small area around the shore the condition might easily be somewhat different. That position will be watched carefully.
The other matter to which the hon. member referred was the extension of territorial waters. I have repeatedly stated in the house that, with regard to the conservation of fish, the three-mile limit was not satisfactory. However, the extension of territorial waters is an international matter and would require agreement by many other nations. The question of the stocks of fish comes within the competency of the international commission for the north Atlantic fisheries, that will be holding its second session in St. Andrews at the end of this month. At the present time the commission is examining the position in area No. 5, which is George's bank. Other areas will receive the attention of the commission from time to time.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Gloucester on his maiden speech. We were glad to hear him and to realize that he is interested in the fisheries of his riding. I wish to assure him that we too are greatly interested in that area. He spoke particularly about insurance for fishermen's boats. He also spoke about lack of assistance. I should like to advise him that in his own county we have given a subsidy to some 38 boats, to a total of approximately $167,000, which was $165 a ton. Every one of those boats is insured. They are insured for protection. The provincial government gives them a loan. We give them a grant. Our grant is insured for a period of five years, but the boat is insured until the provincial loan is paid off. It is therefore possible to get insurance on certain types of boats.
I will agree, however, that there are many smaller boats with gasoline engines on which it is virtually impossible to get insurance; at least the rate for insurance is so high that the fishermen could not afford to carry insurance on a small boat. I should like to inform the hon. member for Gloucester and other hon. members that at the present time

we have three men from our economics branch set aside to study the possibility and the probability of bringing into force insurance on boats.
Personally, I have considered that the lives of the fishermen and the boats they work in are the two main things to be taken care of. If it is at all possible to provide some insurance which I hope will be a three-way insurance; that is, where the fishermen, the provincial government and the federal government take part in providing insurance, at the start, on men's lives and on the boats that they sail in. Later on, if it is possible to include the gear, that can be done but it will probably be well after my time. However, I want everyone to be assured that the lot of these people who harvest this valuable food from the sea is one with which we are concerning ourselves.
The hon. member for Charlotte brought out the idea-and it was referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South-that the $160,000 that is paid as a bounty should be used for insurance purposes. In the hon. member's own riding there are 146 boat owners and 181 fishermen working on the boats, or a total of 327 men, in the county of Charlotte who are getting some of this money. In the whole of the maritime provinces there are 14,358 men. It would be very difficult to get all of these men to agree to cancel their right, which amounts to a little more than $6 apiece; it amounts to $9.55 each. That is what it amounted to last year.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said that it was a variable amount. It is not exactly a variable amount; it is the interest on $4 million. That is the amount on which the interest is based. I think it would be difficult to get an agreement from the 14,358 fishermen that their money should be used to pay for insurance on boats when perhaps a good many of these men do not own any boats at all. There is also $1 a ton on the vessel itself that goes to the vessel owners. They could easily apply that, if they wished, to this purpose. However, it is a matter of their own desire as to whether they would like it to go to pay insurance on their boats. There would be great difficulty in getting all these men to agree to the use of that money for that purpose. I take it that this is not an instance where the majority should rule. In this instance the individual should have some rights.
The hon. member for Charlotte did make a very useful speech. He is a man who knows the fishing industry very well. A good many of the suggestions that he put forward will be seriously considered. He, too, advocated the principle that the $160,000 should be used 55704-217
Supply-Fisheries
for the purpose of insurance. He spoke of the price of sardines. The price of sardines is a competitive one in the tinned fish trade. In the first place, the plants in his own district have to compete with the sardines and can-ners from the state of Maine, and that competition is pretty keen. They likewise have to compete with Norway, Sweden and many other countries that are putting up sardines and have been doing it for quite a long time. Right in the heart of one fishing community that I visited not so long ago I saw Norwegian sardines and our own fishermen ready to buy them. It is a very competitive article, and a good deal of it is sold in the cheaper markets. They are put up in a tin that a man can put into his lunch kit, and that composes the main portion of his lunch.
The hon. member spoke of the competition and implied that some of the canners were not living up to their contracts. 1 think that if any of our Canadian canners were not living up to their contracts the fishermen would very soon complain about it, and they would have recourse to the courts to collect from them. But I think he was referring mainly to the Maine canners, and over them we have of course no control whatever.
The hon. member brought up another matter which I think I should reply to. He mentioned that the amount in the estimates before us is approximately $10 million. It is a little less than that, and he compared that with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, and said that ours is so much smaller. Well, I am not going to say that we are doing everything for the fishermen that we would like to do. I suppose the Minister of Agriculture would say the same about agriculture. But we should at least remember this. The total value of the fisheries to Canada last year, including Newfoundland, was $200 million. On the other hand, the total value of agriculture to Canada is $2 billion. There is a vast difference. If you compare the $10 million that we have with the $60 million that agriculture has, you will see that it is not too far out of line, but more than the $10 million that is in our estimates goes for that type of work. If you want to take in everything that we do for fisheries you will have to examine your estimate books in relation to your various communities or provinces and you will find large sums of money in there for the building of wharves, for breakwaters, for fishermen's floats, and for a great many other items.
The item of $80,625 for price support was referred to. That is only the administrative item. It is not what is actually spent for price support. However, I am not finding

Supply-Fisheries
fault with the hon. member for bringing up these questions. I appreciate it very much, and it will get very careful consideration.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to foreign vessels having a base for their operations on our coasts. This is not a regulation, as was referred to by the hon. member; it is an act of parliament, the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act. I agree with him that it does need revision. He says that it has not been enforced. It was enforced very rigidly up until the beginning of the first war when, by order in council, there was some relaxation. It had been enforced I think rather indifferently between the two wars and since the last war. However, the act is so strenuous in its application that if one of those foreign vessels were picked up we would have no option but to confiscate the vessel itself. That, I think, would be rather unfortunate. When this was brought up about a month ago it was the first time, in my experience. Things have changed considerably since the act was passed. There were days when shore bases in this country were much more valuable to foreign countries than they would be today, when there are modern boats with a much greater tonnage, and with much greater sailing speeds. There is also the difference that, since Newfoundland came into confederation, by the terms of union, Newfoundland was permitted to continue furnishing these boats with supplies.
Then there has been another change. The islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon are owned by France, and they have allowed the boats of some European countries to base there. This is a point that has changed the picture considerably.
We have been asked what we are going to do about the act, and the answer is that we are going to discuss the matter with other departments vitally interested, with a view to a revision of the act. We would hope that this revision of the act, whatever it may be, will be done in sufficient time to enable people on the Nova Scotia and New Brunswick coasts to make preparations to have supplies ready for the boats, should we find it desirable to make the change in the act.
However, this is not something that can be done lightly, because a number of factors are involved. When we give shore rights to a foreign country, we give to them the full advantage Canada has in respect to its proximity to the fishing grounds. In extending this privilege we would be giving away the locational advantage our fishermen have, and, I suggest, we have a right to expect something valuable in return for that.
[Mr. Mayhew.j
Before taking my seat I should like to make one further observation, in the hope that those who are interested will pay some attention to it. We prohibit our own nationals from fishing in their larger boats inside the twelve-mile limit, while foreign boats can come in to the three-mile limit. I would hope that the foreign boats coming in and having the privilege of using our ports would at least recognize the regulations we have placed upon our own draggers and trawlers.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two comments on this first item. The hon. member for Gloucester dealt this morning with some of the problems of the maritime fishermen, and this subject was also discussed by other hon. members, in particular the hon. member for Charlotte and the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
As the first member of the official opposition to speak, following the speech of the hon. member for Gloucester, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate him upon the showing he made this morning. His speech augurs well for the valuable contribution he will be able to make as time goes on.
The minister dealt with certain matters of administration, and referred specifically to the possibility of insurance. His declaration was one which all hon. members will welcome, and which we believe is necessary. Some steps in that direction are past due, and I am glad to know the minister is giving the matter consideration. In my opinion some action should be taken.
Of course that is only part of this general problem confronting the fishermen, and particularly the inshore fishermen, those operating on smaller capital and with the small boats. I noticed a while ago an announcement by the Department of Labour in which it was said that it was impossible to apply unemployment insurance to the fishing industry. I think that is a wise decision; in view of the number of share men operating on the larger boats, and the number operating in smaller boats, I should think it would be virtually impossible to do anything for them that would be beneficial by way of unemployment insurance.
Someone may say that there is a sick mariners fund. Although I have no direct knowledge in the matter, it may well be that the sick mariners fund would serve a useful purpose in respect of those fishermen operating out of Lunenburg, or those other ports where one finds the large trawlers, and other heavy equipment going out for purposes of deep-sea fishing. But this does not apply in respect of line fishermen operating out of the little ports along the coast-or if it does

operate at all, then only in a very few cases. Those men own their own small boats. They simply go out into the bays and return at nights. My understanding is that in order to qualify for treatment they have to be taken sick while aboard, and the fact is that most of them are at home when sickness befalls them. Thus the fund is absolutely useless to them.
I say there should be some study given to working out a program equivalent to that of workmen's compensation. I realize that workmen's compensation is a provincial responsibility, and that it is administered by the provinces. But it must be kept in mind that the fisheries come within the jurisdiction of the federal government. In my view we should make a study of the system. For instance, I have seen fishermen whose hands have been punctured by hooks, and where blood poisoning has set in. Those men have been laid off for months, and without receiving one red cent. Their earning capacity is ruined for the rest of their lives.
I know those fishermen do believe that some such system could be invoked. I would hope that departmental officials might give further consideration to this matter, and that when he speaks again this afternoon the minister might make reference to it. Or, if he would consider the matter, and speak about it at another time, I would be happy then to hear what he would have to say.
The minister made another interesting statement this afternoon when he referred to the draggers. I understood him to say that there was no evidence as yet that the operations of draggers had resulted in a depletion of stocks, but that study would be given to the matter, and if they were satisfied that this depletion had taken place some appropriate action would be taken. I can recall raising this matter of draggers and trawlers three or four years ago when I first came to the House of Commons, and that at that time the then minister gave exactly the same answer. He said there was no evidence that the draggers and trawlers were depleting the stock in any way, but that, if they were, action would be taken.
I notice that in a report which appeared in the Halifax Herald on January 7 of this year the minister's own officials made some comments in this connection. The article quotes Dr. Needier, director of the fisheries biological station at St. Andrews, and Dr. Templeman, director of the fisheries research station of Newfoundland, as making reference to the work which the trawlers and draggers are doing on the banks, and they make reference to the effect on stocks when, for instance, two Spanish trawlers sweep 55704-217i
Supply-Fisheries
together. They make the statement that the evidence indicates that this is prejudicial to the stock of haddock.
I suggest that if in the opinion of experts there is evidence that these trawlers operating on the banks are depleting the haddock stock, it is a fair inference that the smaller draggers operating in narrower waters would also damage the stock. I can assure the minister of this, that it will require all his eloquence, logic and charming personality to convince the fishermen along the bay of Fundy that this is not the result. It may be coincidental with the shortage of haddock, but many of the people down there hold the belief that these draggers and trawlers are definitely prejudicial to the industry.
The minister pointed out a moment ago that our own draggers and trawlers are required to keep twelve miles off the coast, whereas foreign vessels may come within three miles, and that that is a matter to which he has given attention. I think it is time that special attention was given to this matter because, as I have said before and as the minister undoubtedly knows, there are departmental reports to show that at times these boats do come within the three-mile limit and operate close to the shore line, in fact so close that they drag up lobster traps which are set a few hundred feet from the coast. The excuse is always that they have been lost in the fog. I certainly regret that lack of navigational skill which permits them to get lost, and still avoid going on the rocks entirely. The only ones they are putting on the rocks are the fishermen whose gear and fish are being destroyed. I think definite action should be taken in this regard.
Reference was made to the extension of the coastal waters. I think there is a good legal argument, certainly a practical argument which could be advanced for the declaring of the bay of Fundy as being inland waters. I understand certain peace treaties would be involved. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree that in the discussions which took place many years ago between Great Britain, which was then looking after our foreign affairs, and the United States that matter was left open. If the departmental officials would go into this and see that it was raised at a conference I think that they would find that action could be obtained.
While I realize that there is logic and force-in his argument, I hate to accept entirely the statement of the hon. member for Cape Breton South that because this industry is being mechanized the little people are being forced out entirely. I admit that that is true in connection with deep-sea fishing.

Supply-Fisheries
Those of us from Nova Scotia will remember the bitterness of the discussion twenty years or more ago when we had the controversy as between trawlers and schooners and the rest. That matter was settled because of economic necessity; that era is past.
But all along the coast are many small villages which are supported by fishing operations from small boats which go out into the bay of Fundy or probably in waters in other parts of Canada. That phase of the industry cannot be mechanized. You have an ideal situation in the bay of Fundy and if proper steps were taken to stop the operations of trawlers and draggers the small hand-line fisherman would be able to earn his living and support his family and community as he has supported them for generations. With the regulations that now exist and the circumstances under which they now operate, unless something is done all these communities along the bay of Fundy and in the southwestern part of the province are going to be threatened with extinction. I urge that action be taken in this connection.
I do not want to take up the time of the committee any longer except to refer to one other matter which has already been before the house, the damage which was done to the fishing industry last winter by the serious storms which occurred at that time. The minister has referred to the possibility of some insurance scheme being worked out to cover the boats. That would be most helpful, but in this series of storms, which were almost continuous, almost complete economic disaster was faced by fishermen all along the coast of Nova Scotia.
Speeches were made in the house by the hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth, the hon. member for Charlotte, and I think I made a contribution myself, urging that action be taken. I am sorry to see that as far as the main estimates are concerned there is no item which I can relate to the disaster which these people suffered. Possibly something will be included in the supplementary estimates, and I think we should be told whether there will be an item there. We have heard the logical appeals made by hon. members representing various constituencies and some action should be taken.
I was reading a statement made in the other place by an hon. gentleman from New Brunswick who at one time was a cabinet minister in the government of that province, and it certainly was not a Conservative government. He said that in so far as the maritimes are concerned apparently God worked in a different way than for the rest of Canada. When an act of God occurred down there it was considered to be the fault

of the people and nothing could be done about it, whereas the government apparently felt it had some responsibility for the acts of the Divinity in the rest of Canada. That was a statement made in the other place.
In answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth the parliamentary assistant said that the matter was under investigation. Then the minister stated that there had been no request from Nova Scotia with regard to this. I have here a long and indignant statement by the minister of trade and industry of Nova Scotia which deals with the whole situation. He states that this matter is the responsibility of the federal government and that he has asked that action be taken.
It is true, as some have suggested this morning, that this industry has not received the same support which other industries have received, but I do not agree for a moment with the hon. member for Charlotte that, because agriculture has received certain treatment, fishing should receive parallel treatment or be considered on the same basis. Farmers suffer crop failures, and at least in the east they do not receive any money for it. They suffer from storms and various other things and receive no money. I think the minister was right when he said that in so far as the economic value of the product was concerned, agriculture was not receiving proportionately more than fishing.
If an economic disaster such as this had occurred to some other industry in some other part of Canada I think it would have been received much more sympathetically than this particular situation. I think the minister should state just where this matter stands, just what is being done or what will be done with respect to it. Scores and scores of fishermen have lost virtually all their capital. They have lost their boats, they have lost their gear, and in many cases, as the Minister of Public Works well knows, the wharves in their villages were lost. We do hope that some of these will be replaced so they can carry on.
This matter should receive consideration. We have heard it said that this industry is an orphan, but this government which is now in power should look after it. We realize that the minister is taking an interest in this industry and has travelled around the country, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South has said, probably more than any other minister. But no matter how sympathetic or how intellectual the consideration given to this matter may be, that alone will not solve the economic problems of these people. I ask the minister and the department to give these matters careful consideration and see that action is taken at the proper time.

Mr. Chairman, I think I should answer the hon. member right now. The province of Nova Scotia asked that a survey be made by the department of the storm losses in that province. That was completed last month. I am now informed that there has arrived at my office an official request from Nova Scotia for assistance. We have not had time to consider that so I do not know what it contains.
At the earlier request of the provincial government a thorough survey was made of the losses. The bulk of the losses were made up of lobster traps. The number of traps reported lost in the storm is given at 155,000, or 30 per cent of the total owned by fishermen. These traps would be worth about $1 million but it is understood that many of the traps lost were old. There are of course always some losses, so that only a proportion of this year's loss can be considered to be above normal. The government has just received a submission from the provincial government based on the facts as now known.
The lobster catch in Nova Scotia for the first four months of this vear was 4 [DOT] 7 million pounds as compared with 5-7 million pounds in the same period in 1951. With better prices, however, the value of the catch this year was $2,256,000 compared with $2,121,000 a year ago. That is the position today and I can assure hon. members that due consideration will be given to the provincial government's request.

I just want to address a few remarks to the minister as the Minister of Fisheries and also, I hope, as a minister from British Columbia.
As he will realize, our province is having its share of difficulties these days. We seem to have strikes in lumber and amongst our carpenters, and there is also threat of a strike in fisheries out there. We have all those troubles which have also been complicated by what I might suggest was "hoof-and-Hansell" disease out there. I know the minister will be particularly interested and probably the fisheries research board will be interested to note that they catch the biggest crop of suckers with bait of just straight corn.

However, getting back to a serious vein, I must say that the threat of the fisheries strike out there is very serious and it seems to me that both sides would be very interested in the remarks which the minister made today. I felt, however, that the minister was somewhat reticent. I can quite understand his not wanting to take part in what appears to be a labour dispute, but it seems to me that with the type of fishery there is in British Columbia it is a little different
Supply-Fisheries
from the ordinary fisheries dispute. I do not think either the fishermen or the operators out there can claim any fishery. I think the people of Canada can claim that it is one of their assets. It would seem to me that the minister might have gone considerably further than he did this morning and given both sides of the dispute some factual information which he must have and which is available either in his department or through the Department of Trade and Commerce who always have surveys of market conditions in Canada. They will know the true picture of the stocks of canned salmon on hand. It seemed to me that on going into a new packing season with this very substantial carryover we would all be very interested to know just how he feels about it.
As I said, I do not feel that he would be taking part in what might ordinarily be termed an industrial dispute if he were to give us that. As the minister realizes, fish are not like timber. If we have a strike in the timber industry naturally we have a tie-up of timber while the strike goes on, but that is not so with salmon on the Fraser river. I am speaking here particularly of sockeye salmon.. Great steps have been taken in the conservation and propagation of the run on the Fraser river so it seems to me we should see what can be done to assist, as this asset belongs to the Canadian people as a whole. The minister knows that if these beds get more salmon than they can take there is actual harm done to the fishery.
As we all know the Americans are going to get their share of the catch and I would like to be sure that we, through our fisheries department, are acting in the interest of the Canadian people by trying to take what steps are possible to ensure that Canada gets its share this year, whether or not the fish operators and the fishermen get together out there. I would be very anxious to see the minister have a senior representative of his department out there while the negotiations are going on. I would like him to provide some factual information regarding the market, which I think would be very helpful in this case.
I was glad when the minister replied to the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena the other night. I too feel that fishermen in many cases pay sales tax on commercial gear when they should not have to. I realize that there are difficulties of administration of which we are quite well aware, and I am sure the department is doing everything possible to see those difficulties are adjusted. I would just ask the minister to use his good offices to see that sales tax is removed from commercial fishing gear in every possible case.

Supply-Fisheries
Coming from the Pacific coast I think I should say a word about the passing of Mr. Frank Tait of the minister's department, who was district supervisor at Nanaimo and who served the department with distinction for so many years. It is a matter of great regret to us there that he passed away so suddenly.
In conclusion I would like to commend the officials of the department for what I maintain is very efficient administration on the Pacific coast. That is the only place where I am familiar with their activities, and I can assure you it is excellent.

speechtext:
This morning the minister referred to the carryover of the pack on the west coast. While he was not able to say the extent of that carryover it is obvious that it is very considerable. I wonder if the minister could tell us now what steps his department is taking to assist that situation, particularly in view of the difficult labour situation which has arisen on the Pacific coast and to which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has just referred. I wonder whether every possible endeavour has been made to find avenues by which the carryover can be disposed of. It occurs to me that possibly the armed forces should have an opportunity to use some of that carryover, and I would like to know if the minister has investigated that possibility. Would he tell us what steps his department is taking?
I would also like to add my tribute to Mr. Tait, who passed away only a few weeks ago. He was known to all of us on the Pacific coast and was very highly regarded not only by officials of the department but by the fishermen of the whole area.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
I am sure the family of Mr. Tait will be very pleased to learn of the kind remarks by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Nanaimo. Similar remarks have already been passed on to the family by myself and by the department.
May I at this moment refer to another member of the department whom we lost and who has been a very close friend for a number of years. I speak of Mr. Hanson, who was a member of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission. Olof Hanson, once a member of this house, made a considerable contribution to British Columbia and to Canada. Although he had a good living out of Canada, he made sure that wherever he was, no matter what position he held, he left the country better than he found it.
Both hon. members have spoken about our canned salmon position. Last week the canned salmon operators had two representatives in Ottawa, and we spent a good many

hours with them going over their problems and canvassing any plans that might be helpful to them. They left the city the night before last, and I am quite sure they are satisfied that if there is anything this department can do we will do it.
I did not mention the amount of the carryover, because I do not think they would appreciate that. It is not something they would reveal in the ordinary course of business, so I do not think it would be right to mention it here. Anyone who is interested can easily make a fairly close calculation and see that it is a considerable amount. Last year the pack was a little over 2 million cases. Because of the exchange situation the industry will not be able to send any more salmon to the United Kingdom this year. A large sum of money has been spent in trying to promote the sale of salmon in Canada. The industry has spent almost $350,000 and the individual canners are spending another $350,000, making a total of $700,000 spent in promoting the sale of canned salmon within Canada. As a result of that expenditure considerably more than the usual amount of canned salmon has been marketed domestically.
If the expected pack of approximately a million and a half cases is realized this year, that is providing the fishermen go to work, there could be a substantial carryover again at this time next year. I do not think that I should say any more than that. I believe everyone in British Columbia realizes that the stocks are high. They realize also that the price of canned salmon is high, and that it is difficult to make sales at high prices. I believe that with the good judgment of all concerned they will be able to get together and straighten this out without a strike. I do not feel I should say more than that at the present time.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
I should like to avail myself of this opportunity to say that I appreciate the work which has been done by the fisheries department, and also to pay tribute to the minister himself. As one who has the honour of representing possibly the third largest riding in Canada, and the one with the longest shore line, I think that my remarks at this time are in order. I should like to refer particularly to the Labrador coast, and to point out to the minister the need for protecting the salmon rivers. I would suggest that fishery guardians be appointed there, as is the case in Newfoundland.
I should like also to mention the serious decline in the Labrador fishery. In 1935 that fishery produced about 400,000 quintals of fish, that is floaters and shore fishermen together. Last year I believe the catch was down to less than one-third of that, or

approximately 130,000 quintals. That is a serious decline in the Labrador fishery. As the house may remember I brought this matter to the attention of the department last year when the fisheries estimates were under consideration. I do not know what can be done about the matter, but I believe that last year the shore fishery produced about
700,000	quintals. In view of the extent of the trawling and dragging operations which are being conducted on the banks of Newfoundland, I believe we can reasonably look forward to the time when our fishermen will have to go farther afield in order to secure the catch of fish needed by the Canadian people, in fact by the whole world, as a source of food.
So far as Labrador is concerned, I should like to point out that every spring seal fishing takes place along the Labrador coast and the strait of Belle Isle. The fishermen who prosecute this fishery take the pelts and the fat, but leave a tremendous amount of good food on the ice floes which they are unable to utilize. The report of the fisheries department and the research board just came to hand yesterday and I have not been able to make a close study of it, but it does reveal the tremendous amount of research which is taking place in this regard. I believe something could be worked out whereby we could utilize some of this wholesome protein food which now goes to the bottom of the ocean. I can vouch for the food value of the kidneys and livers of these young seals, and there is a great deal of food value in the rest of the carcass. If it were only utilized for poultry or dog food, at least some way should be found to use these resources which are now sinking to the bottom of the ocean.
We are very thankful for the deficiency payments which have been made by the department to the Newfoundland fishermen. It appears that far-reaching changes may be in the offing for the fisheries of Newfoundland, so a word or two in this regard may not be out of order. I should like to say a word about the marketing organization in Newfoundland which is known as NAFEL, the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited. When we realize the chaotic conditions that existed in the free marketing of fish in the European market and the cutthroat competition, and then see the orderly marketing which we have through NAFEL we are impressed with the wisdom of keeping such an organization, even though it may need some reorganization in order that the maximum return will be forthcoming to assure our producers of being properly reimbursed for their labours.
Supply-Fisheries
Another matter I should like to mention, Mr. Chairman, is that of unemployment insurance. I am not unmindful of the difficulties which are in the way of working out a suitable scheme of unemployment insurance for fishermen; but I want to go on record as saying that I do not consider that this matter defies solution. Where there is a will there is a way. I believe it is possible to work out a scheme whereby unemployment insurance may be made available for the fishermen.
I realize that this year a change has taken place with regard to the value of our exports to the European markets, in view of the change in the currency situation. This year instead of our fish being sold for sterling it is to be sold for dollars. I hope the minister will see that dollars will be available to the European buyers so the exporters will be able to get the necessary currency in exchange for their fish.
There are certain other matters that I should like to mention. For instance, I think that additional investigation of the banks off Newfoundland and Labrador should be followed up. We are looking forward to the report of the fisheries development committee.
There is also the matter of the extension of the territorial waters of Canada. I think it was only last year that some of the Norwegian sealing steamers which engaged in the seal fishery here in Canadian waters came within the three-mile limit and picked up seals. I could not say whether or not those were their own seals which they had taken, panned and flagged and which had been driven, as were the ships, within the three-mile limit. The whole matter needs to be gone into. I believe that possibly a suitable treaty or convention could be arranged with Norway and the other countries whose fishermen obtain the advantage of this natural resource upon which our fishermen have to depend in order to get their livelihood.
In my district the losses, by fishermen were serious last year as a result of that December storm. I am glad some insurance will be worked out for their protection.
Another matter I wish to mention is the need for a bait depot in my district at La Scie. I should like to point out to the minister one other thing, as I have already done. I understand that the site was bought or secured in order to put a bait depot there, but so far I cannot get any further definite promise of a bait depot at La Scie. I should like to point out that not far from La Scie there are two islands, namely the Horse islands, and just across the neck of land in Notre Dame bay there is a settlement of fishermen called Shoe Cove; and it is impossible for the fishermen

Supply-Fisheries
there to have any large wharf or facilities other than their stages which they use to land their catches of fish. I should like to impress upon the minister the necessity of getting a bait depot for these people. I am not one who would advocate unnecessary expenditures; but I would say this is a necessity for our people.
While the fisheries are declining in Newfoundland and, as was pointed out by the minister this morning, there is a drawing away from the fisheries to other more profitable avenues of employment, as is quite natural, nevertheless we realize that the fishing industry has been looked upon in Newfoundland as the backbone of the country in the past. We must protect these men, and we want to do something to encourage them.
There is just one other point I want to suggest, Mr. Chairman, and it is this. I would ask the minister, in his reply, to put on record the details with regard to the bounty of $165 a ton which is being paid for long-liners. I believe this is the way in which our fisheries will be developed in the main in the future. As I said before, I am looking forward to the report of the fisheries development committee which has been functioning for a long time and has put a great deal of hard work into its report. We all look forward to that report with interest, feeling that it will bring forth some sort of plan which will be most helpful to the fishermen in Newfoundland.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the remarks made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I believe that he and I, along with the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, represent most of the west coast salmon fishermen. His idea with regard to the department having a responsible official doing the negotiating in connection with the strike that may happen on Sunday is good. It seems to me that if these men-the united fishermen's union and the industry-approached this matter with any kind of common sense and with the feeling that they wanted to settle the strike, it could be done in about half an hour. In Steveston in the municipality of Richmond we are faced with having some 1,500 boats tied up on the shore. Those fishermen have large families. The economic results of this possible strike in my riding are going to be severe, as they will in Comox-Alberni and in Coast-Capilano.
I know it is a provincial matter, as the Minister of Labour told me the other day in reply to a question of mine in the house with reference to the lumber strike. But there again common sense perhaps goes beyond legal limits. If a senior official from the

fisheries department cannot hold a watching brief-and I quite understand why he could not do so, and I quite understand why the Minister of Fisheries would not want to become involved in what is perhaps a purely domestic matter-I think something can be done in this House of Commons at least to help in the settlement of the strike before it happens. As I say, most of the fishermen are in these three constituencies. It is quite understandable why the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance could not go to the coast even though he might want to do so. However, I think some of us private members who are interested should offer to sit around the table with the fishermen and the industry, should they want us to do so, before this matter comes to a definite strike. I want to suggest to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that he and I should offer or volunteer and that if our services are requested in this matter in an unofficial capacity, we should make ourselves available to both the industry and the fishermen on the west coast.

speechtext:

Yesterday I put a question to the minister to which I should like to have had a more definite answer today, with reference to the extension of twelve days being granted in the month of July. I do not wish to dictate to the department or even tell them that it should be done. If the inspector down there goes to the fishermen, as I understood the minister to say today is to be done, and the fishermen say they should have that extension, well, they should have it. I would rather argue this season for some compensation for the extremely heavy losses they have had this year. Take the people of Prince Edward Island, on the north shore and on the south shore. There the season opens May 1. Their first loss this year was from ice conditions, something that rarely happens. On top of that they had the worst storms of the season. Out of some 12,000 traps the fishermen put out from Rustico harbour I understand that over 6,000 were lost. That is 50 per cent of the total number of traps and gear they put out. On the south side, where the storm was not quite so bad, they lost 25 per cent

of their gear. That does not happen every season, but it did happen this year. If the fishermen do not get their traps repaired, or if they do not know in time that they are going to have an extension of twelve extra days in July they will not have any traps fit to put out. Therefore I urge the minister and the department, if they are going to make that decision, to make it soon so the fishermen can put out some extra gear to take advantage of the twelve days extra time, or whatever extension they may have.
There are several other matters I might speak about, but as the time is going along and there are many other estimates to come up I think perhaps I shall leave my further remarks until a little later except to say a word about draggers and the waste that some other hon. members have said is caused by the draggers. I understand that in my province the department is supporting draggers and perhaps putting them into business where there was never any dragger fishing until last year. As one hon. member said, if the draggers are going to put the shore fisheries out of business it should be thoroughly considered before any action is taken, so our shore fishermen will not lose what at the present time is their livelihood.
Quite a few hon. members spoke about the bounty this afternoon. I understand that the bounty is more or less a trust fund which could not be taken and used, without the proper legislation, for anything but a bounty. When we come to that item I hope the minister will give us a little bit of the history of the bounty money, where it comes from and so forth. We know how it has been spent; it goes out as a bounty. If the minister will give us some information about that bounty when he replies it will settle some of the arguments as to whether or not it could be used for insurance.

3444

I want to say to the minister and the department that I hope this season, whatever the catch is, they will have it properly processed instead of having a portion of the seals processed and the others dragged along at a very low price. I notice that this year, for instance, those processed in St. Louis by the Fouke company sold on an average for about $66 more than those processed in the other place.
I have warned the department about that for the last seven years and I hope they now have definitely changed their policy and that we will not have to compliment them in the same manner another year. We hope to see their earnings improve; and I think the committee would be very glad to find out from the minister the amount of profit this fur seal trade is bringing in.
I have another point on this matter of fur seals. A few days ago I drew to the attention of the minister the fact that Japan wanted to get back into this treaty and get a share of the fur seal business. Whatever the minister does on behalf of his department and Canada, let him not give away one per cent or one single skin. If the Americans wish to give their share or to give any amount we cannot stop them. We are now entitled to 20 per cent, so let that not get out of our hands. We need that 20 per cent. Do not be influenced by anyone who says Japan should have 5 per cent. Japan at one time had the opportunity and abused it. Now let her get that amount from the United States if she wants to, but I would like the minister and the department to stand firm and not give away one per cent let alone 5 per cent of our share of the fur seals.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Does the minister feel that he can usefully comment on the observations made by the hon. gentleman?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
The member for Queens first asked what was the revenue from this source. It was a gross of $772,507.84 last year. We paid to the Canadian government $482,245.52 in duty, which left a net of $290,262.32; but the revenue to Canada was $772,507.84.
In connection with the remarks the hon. member made about Japan, I believe Japan has made application but the matter has not yet been given consideration. Those remarks will be in our minds when any negotiations are going on.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Can the minister give us assurance now that the processing of our fur seals will all be done at one place, in St. Louis?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
The first year I was Minister of Fisheries there was quite an agitation to

give a Canadian firm a chance to prove whether they could properly process seal skins in Canada and thus create a manufacturing industry. We did allow a Toronto firm a considerable number of skins to see what they could do. That has not turned out to be a success up to date, so they are not processing at all. We still have some skins in England with Martin's. They will be finished and sent to Canada. If they turn out to be as good as the St. Louis Fouke skins we may try them out with some more. However, my instructions to the department this year have been that all the skins we take this year should go to the Fouke company at St. Louis for processing and dyeing. Further than that, we have asked them to process enough that we can reduce our inventory of skins at St. Louis.

Item agreed to.
Protection branch-
148. Operation and maintenance, $2,747,294.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether this is the right time to ask the minister a question about hatcheries. I regret that I was not here this morning, when I understand the minister spoke about the fish hatcheries in the maritimes. I wonder if he would mind letting me know whether any consideration has been given to the establishment of a salmon or trout hatchery in Newfoundland.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I answered the question this morning and I think the hon. member will find the answer in Hansard.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: The only reason I mention this is that I understand the minister said there was no work done last year in the maritimes on hatcheries.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I did not say no work was done; I said no new hatcheries were built in the maritimes last year. When I first saw them the hatcheries were in a pretty run-down condition and I thought they should be repaired and at least put in presentable condition. That was done, but no new hatcheries were built. Trout hatcheries in Newfoundland, as well as in some other places, are the responsibility of the provincial government. As far as salmon hatcheries are concerned they have not proved adequate to meet needs. We think the policy of clearing and improving the ascent to the fish beds is a better way of increasing salmon production in Newfoundland as well as in other places.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
I must thank the minister for going to the trouble of again saying what he said this morning, but I

would like to draw attention to the report of the department for 1950-51 where it says:
Thirty-three new outdoor concrete ponds, each with a capacity of up to 50,000 salmon or trout fingerlings, were constructed at hatcheries throughout Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
I was referring to work in 1950-51, unless he tells us it is impossible to learn what is being done in 1951. It is further stated in the report that:
Operations were carried on at thirteen main hatcheries . . .
Do I understand from the minister that the policy of salmon hatcheries is being abandoned notwithstanding the extra work which was done in that season?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: The concrete you refer to was put on the bottoms of the pools. They were mud bottoms, and we put in concrete bottoms as an improvement of the hatcheries.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: On that point, Mr. Chairman, on page 21 of the report these figures are given: speckled trout, 12,045,408; brown trout, 30,655; rainbow trout, 147,176. They must have been planting these small trout there.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Under the terms of the union Newfoundland agreed to look after the fresh water streams, but our department is responsible in the maritimes.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: There are two questions I would like to ask on item 148. In Nova Scotia a great many guardians are employed over a period of six months but actually they are only paid for a period of perhaps four months. It is rather difficult for a man to give up some employment he might have, thinking he is going to be employed for six months and then receive remuneration for only four months. I think perhaps even where the water might be low and fish not very numerous the employment of those guardians should be continued.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Well, that is something new to me. I never heard that we were engaging people for six months and only paying them four months' salary. I have not the answer here, but I assure the hon. member I shall look into it.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I have another question that comes under this item. Has there been an open season on Arctic char?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: There has been no open season for Arctic char; we have given special permits in that connection.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
Will the minister comment briefly on the boats which are available for protective service on the east coast, and particularly for the western part of my province. Last year I think there was one called the Cygnus which was available, in addition to
Supply-Fisheries
an older one that was in such bad shape the captain thought it was unsafe to take out in stormy weather. Only these two ships were available for work around the southwestern part of the province, so I should like to know if the minister would make a brief statement listing the number of ships which are available for that service.
I noticed also in the details for this item-
I do not want to inquire about a lot of details -that apparently this year we are employing 39 captains as compared with 42 for the year before. I presume that the word "captains" refers to sea captains and not to vessels. We have 39 full-time employees, which is 3 less than last year, yet the amount for this year is $116,868 as compared with $97,104 for last year.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
We have eight boats in all
available in this section.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Could the minister name them,, please?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: There is the Cygnus, Lacuna, Limanda, A. Halkett, Gilbert, Venning, Modiolus and the Mya.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Where are they based? From what ports do they operate?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: There is the Gilbert at Lunenburg, the Cygnus at Halifax; the Lacuna at Halifax and the Limanda in the Digby-Yar-mouth area; the Modiolus in the Digby Neck-St. Mary's bay area; the A. Halkett is across at Cape Breton, the Mya and the Venning are in the Northumberland straits.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: In this same connection, I find we appear to be providing money for 100 engineers. I should like to ask the minister if there is actually a need for 100 engineers, and for what purpose are they used?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I think the hon. member is taking in all the engineers throughout Canada, including Newfoundland and the Atlantic coast. In that event he would be about right.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Will the minister explain the increase in the salaries for captains? Perhaps there was an automatic increase, but I just noticed that apparently there was a reduction by three in the number of captains, but an increase of about $20,000.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: That is due to a salary revision by the Department of Labour.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Do I understand from the minister that there is a need for 100 engineers in operating the boats used by the Department of Fisheries?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
We have approximately 70 ships protecting the whole area, some of which are quite large and require more than

Supply-Fisheries
one engineer. Some have two engineers and some three, depending upon their size and their sailings.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question about the increase in operation and maintenance. There was an increase of $146,286 in this item for the protection branch under "field services" the increase in operation and maintenance is $457,903. I think the minister should give an explanation of that large increase in one year.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: The hon. member will notice there is quite a list of employees in this protection branch, and the increase here is the increase allowed in the revision of salaries last year.

153.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $193,190.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: This item refers to fish culture and development work, operation and maintenance. I recognize that this is a very important service, but a large sum of money seems to be needed. There is a great necessity for fish culture work in Nova .Scotia and the maritime provinces in order to build up these places as tourist attractions. I should like to have a statement from the minister concerning what is being done in expanding that work, and how many fish hatcheries there are in Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
This is an important department, in fact one of our most important. Its functions include stream surveys, stream improvement and control, predator control, reduction and elimination, and modified hatchery production procedures as an aid to maintaining and increasing stocks of fish. It includes also field administration of oyster and clam culture in the maritime provinces. The main functions are operation of experimental oyster farms to develop farming techniques based on scientific research and their demonstration.
The number of hatcheries in Nova Scotia are: main hatcheries 7, salmon ponds 3, rearing stations 5, or a total of 15.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
I notice that in this item there is a decrease of $9,000. This is an important branch. I was wondering whether the minister had any statement to give to the committee as to what success is attending their efforts in selling canned salmon. I was particularly interested in the comment made

by the hon. member for Nanaimo today with regard to the armed services. About a year ago, from the answer to a question of mine, it seemed that the armed forces were eating comparatively little canned salmon. A commodity of this kind is easily stored, and it is of high quality. I noticed particularly that our armed services were eating the most expensive type of canned salmon. I would have thought possibly the department would be able to influence the cooks or the quartermaster's officers to use more of our product than they do, particularly the pink variety of salmon. It certainly is competitive with other protein foods and is economical.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
The reduction in this item is not real because we are going to have to ask for something more in the supplementary estimates in order to provide for the fisheries cook book which I think most hon. members have seen. There has been wide circulation and favourable acceptance by the trade generally of that book. We therefore must have an extra amount in the supplementaries to make up what we thought we were going to be able to get along without.
The hon. member for Nanaimo spoke about the use of salmon in the armed forces. I think I am quite safe in saying that matter is being arranged. I had the experience of sampling some Russian salmon on one of our boats in Korea. I was able to talk the matter over with the minister here and I think in future our troops, wherever they are, will be able to get canned salmon.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: The minister was also asked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni how this program was working out. I wonder if he can tell us about that. I do not know as yet where the experimental kitchen is. I should like to see it some time.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I will give the hon. member an invitation now to come down and have a sample from our kitchen.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Today or tomorrow?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I will give hon. members a general invitation, as long as too many of them do not come down at a time. Last year we asked a great many parties to come down-or at least the ladies did-to have a demonstration in the kitchen. I would say our diet kitchen is one of our most effective pieces of work, having regard to the work they are doing not only here in Ottawa but from one end of Canada to the other. I think it is having a good effect.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
If I can get an invitation by rising to speak I will certainly do so. I want to commend the minister for the work which

has been done by the consumer branch. I think it is something which is well worth while. On both sea coasts I think we are conscious of the fact that this country has not appreciated all the possibilities with regard to the preparation and distribution of fish. I believe real leadership has been given in this matter up to the present time. I think the minister and the officials who have been distributing the literature or working on this matter deserve commendation. I should like to see greater emphasis placed upon it.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I agree that this department is doing important work. I want to join my colleague in commending the minister and the officials for the excellent work they have done in the last two or three years. I want to point out, however, that there is still some room for further development and extension of the work of this department with regard to making fish menus more acceptable to the people, especially to tourists who come to the maritime provinces. Hardly a tourist who comes to our part of the maritime provinces but looks forward to getting tasty menus of native fish. There is a great deal more to be done. I want to commend the minister and his department for what they have done and for what they are endeavouring to do.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Will the minister tell us where that kitchen is or where we have to go?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: The kitchen is in the basement of the west block. You will find the kitchen itself much better than the path to it.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I just want to rise and join other hon. members in complimenting the minister and his officials on the work done under this item. I think it is one thing being done by the fisheries department that is stirring the imagination of many people in Canada. I have heard a number of women express the opinion that it is an extremely effective way of promoting fish sales in this country.

155.	To provide for the destruction of harbour and gray seals, $45,000.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: What was the bounty paid per seal last year and how much bounty was paid for seals destroyed in Prince Edward Island?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-

In Nova Scotia it was
995, $5,780; in Prince Edward Island, 232, $1,505; New Brunswick, 287, $1,895; British Columbia, 279, $13,955 or a total of $23,135.
Supply-Fisheries

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: The bounty is $10?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: $10 for adults and $5 for pups for the maritime provinces.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
Is there any way use could be made of the oil if they were taken in?
I understand that $10 is paid on the snout and that no use is made of the rest of the carcass in any way. Could the oil be extracted? It should be good for something.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: It would be impossible to get them in sufficient volume to be of any use. You get a seal here and there. Before you would get them collected the seals would not be fit to use.

speechtext: They are processed in Newfoundland and it would be quite easy for anyone to get a skin.

speechtext: From Newfoundland. I have not the address. Any of the Newfoundland people could probably give it to the hon. member. Perhaps the hon. member for St. John's West would like to give it to him.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-

Fisheries research board-
156.	Headquarters administration, $92,794.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is pleasing to hear coming from the opposite side such words of praise for the Minister of Fisheries and his staff. Just recently some 50 members of the house had an opportunity to visit Halifax and the experimental station down there under the leadership of Dr. Beatty and his staff and Mr. O. F. Mackenzie. We should like to commend the minister and the deputy at this time for the fine work that has been done.
Does the minister consider that we are making satisfactory progress in the prevention of bacteria spoilage that normally occurs in fish?

Supply-Fisheries

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: I would not like to answer that question; I do not know. We are doing the best we can. I do not think we will ever get to the stage where we will be satisfied with what we are doing.

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: Yesterday I received a copy of the annual report of the fisheries research board of Canada for 1951; I spent most of last night reading it, and I found it very interesting. I would certainly like to compliment the fisheries board on the very fine report they put out and on the work they are doing. I notice that on page 5 it is recommended that a much larger ocean-going vessel is urgently needed for work on the banks in northern waters. Is it the policy of the government this year to have that vessel built?

maintopic: ARTICLES USED BY COMMERCIAL FISHERMEN WHICH ARE NOT DUTIABLE UNDER THE BRITISH PREFERENTIAL OR M.F.N. TARIFF AND WHICH ARE EXEMPT FROM SALES TAX-
speechtext: We have some money in the votes for the plan of a boat, not for the actual construction. We shall have to wait until next year for that.

If he can comment on it now, well and good; if not, I should like to hear from him later.
As he knows, the scallop fishery in the bay of Fundy, emanating from the constituency of Annapolis-Kings, is the largest in Canada and one of the largest in the world, and is of tremendous importance to that whole area. Recently a boat operated by his department, and I believe coming out of St. Andrews, has been fishing or dragging for scallops. Instead of using a conventional ring of 23 inches they have been experimenting with a ring of 3J inches. I have had this matter up with some of the officials of his department and have been told by them-and I accept their word absolutely-that this is simply an experiment which is being carried on and it may not have any particular merit whatsoever. However, it has caused a great deal of concern to many of the fishermen, because from the information I have received the cost of this new ring would be very much in excess of that of the old ring. I believe the boat operated for about thirty days and they caught about 3,200 pounds of scallops. Scallop fishermen would starve to death if they had to operate a ring of that size.
