maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a very brief statement that I would like to put on the record at this time.
The several divisions of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys have a long career of accomplishment in the development of Canada's natural resources. In its several branches we have had and now have men of outstanding qualification who have devoted their lives to the fascinating work of unlocking the storehouse of Canada's resources.
From the discussions that have occurred in this house during the last few weeks I take it that we have quite a number of hon. members who are experts in mining. Those who are not experts are already informed of the work of this department through the publication of the "Summary of Activities in 1951" that has been distributed to all hon. members. If any have not read this publication as yet I would commend it to them, because I think it gives a very concise and complete summary of the activities of our department. This pamphlet was released because of frequent requests from hon. members for information on the activities of the department.
Arising from the rapid expansion of the industry we are now serving, this department has carried out during the last year-and we are planning to carry out this year-one of the largest programs of field work, research work, map making, tests and investigation that we have ever had. Because of the urgent need for minerals that are vital to our defence effort emphasis in recent years has been more particularly on mining and metallurgical problems of economic importance. The work of surveys and exploration has spread out into new areas and has caused an exceptionally large demand for surveys of this department including mapping.
Coupled with this industrial expansion are the requirements of the defence services in


geography, geology, topographical and hydrographic mapping and metallurgy. Much of the assistance given in the discovery of mineral deposits and in developing new mines is indirect, because it is the consistent policy of this department not to compete with or duplicate the services of private industry or provincial governments. However, there are many services that can be properly performed by the government of Canada.
As an introduction to these estimates I just wish to give a brief explanation of the functions of the five branches that make up the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
The surveys and mapping branch supplies the fundamental maps on which all surveys and developments are based. The geological survey of Canada provides through maps and reports the geological information derived from field studies which give clues to the mineral-bearing formations and structures. These maps and reports are a prime necessity for the prospector in his search for minerals. The mines branch has as its broad function the development of processes for the treatment of ores and fuels and of methods of use for many industrial minerals. It deals also with metallurgy in reference to requirements of national defence and of industry. The geographical branch established only a few years ago is proving to be a useful service to many departments of government and to the general public. It conducts field surveys in various parts of Canada and compiles topical studies in Canadian and foreign geography. It also is assembling data for the production of a new atlas of Canada. The dominion observatory has several functions which may be listed as follows: positional astronomy for the determination of precise time; stellar physics or the study of the physical processes going on in the atmosphere; terrestrial magnetism; seismology or the study of earthquakes; astrophysics or the studies of the meteors and the physical nature of the stars.
The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is finding it difficult to keep abreast of the greatly increasing needs of the mining and metallurgical industries and the increased demands for more maps and for more mapping and charting. The department is striving to give the best service possible by concentrating its attention on areas or on problems in the forefront of mineral development, and by giving priority to minerals and problems of current strategic importance.
The hon. member for Peace River suggested that it might save some time and some discussion if I were to give a breakdown of the increase shown in our vote this year. There is a total increase in the vote of $2,803,078. Of this, emergency gold mining assistance is taking $1,300,000. Salary increases and

statutory increases in salary amount to $1,150,000. That leaves a net increase in expenditures amounting to $353,078. That represents only 1 [DOT] 6 per cent increase over the 1952 estimates of expenditure, other than the items mentioned.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South made a reference recently to the work of the geological survey branch of our department. His remarks are reported on page 3280 of Hansard. He cites a request that was made through him to our department for an airborne magnetic survey of an area in Nova Scotia for a private company. It is the policy of this department not to compete with or duplicate the efforts of private industry or of provincial governments. Several companies are equipped to do commercial magnetometer surveys. Their services are available to private companies. The geological survey of Canada has conducted airborne magnetometer surveys since 1949. They are conducted, however, on a broad regional basis, and in no case has a survey been undertaken for an individual enterprise in competition with private consultants or operators.
The airborne magnetometer is to some extent still an experimental device. The policy of this department has been that of investigating the greatest possible number of geological formations over wide areas, in order to study and appraise the value of the results obtained and to correlate the results with the known geological and geophysical data in the areas. Our activities to date in this regard have been in the regions where known geological and geophysical characteristics are most favourable for correlation of results.

I do not suppose that ever before in the history of the human race has such a challenge been put to so few people, Mr. Chairman, as the challenge which the development of our natural resources puts to the 14 million of us who call ourselves Canadians. The possibilities of mineral development in Canada absolutely beggar description. Never has any country shown so much of what lies under its surface as has Canada in recent years, and it is becoming more and more of a challenge to us as new instruments of recovery are developed and perfected.
Before going on with my rather brief remarks, because as I have said this subject is probably as important as the development of the Atlantic pact, I should like to say that our civilization has progressed at a geometric rate. The stone age took many hundreds of thousands of years; the bronze age took a few thousand years; the iron age took a few hundred years; the steel age could possibly be measured in decades, and the
19, 1952	3455
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys atomic age which we are in now could be measured in years. I do not speak tonight as a technical man. Long ago I gave up my practice as an engineer. I speak as a citizen of a country that is just on the verge of becoming one of the really great nations of the world, and becoming so because of the development of its natural resources.
At the outset I shall try to give a little credit for the great work that is being done by the scientific, engineering and technical personnel of this department. Today the men who have the skills of the directors of this department are constantly offered remuneration not twice but frequently many times what they are being paid in the government service. I refer to men like Dr. Hume, the director-general of scientific services; Mr. Bell, head of the geological surveys; Mr. Parsons, of the mines branch; Mr. Watson of the geographical branch and Mr. Miller of the surveys and mapping branch. I should like to see some consideration given to the men who have these skills, which are so important to the development of this country, so they could receive rewards for their services at least in part commensurate with what they could command in private industry. The legal profession has the ability to require payment for services rendered, even while the members of that profession are acting as members of this house. I should like to see consideration given these men and all the others who have technical skills which are so vital to us, to ensure that their remuneration is in line with what they could command in private industry.
Turning to the work of the department, I do not think the people of Canada are aware of what has been happening in Canada since the last war. I do not propose to go into the matter in any detail, but I want to give one or two examples of the sort of thing we have developed. There is today a practice which is known technically as shoran which permits the rapid mapping of vast territories by trilateration with a degree of accuracy which is amazing even when compared with the old triangulation system we were taught as students many years ago. I believe that is a Canadian development or one which was largely perfected in Canada. That one development has meant much to the mapping of our country, particularly to that part of it which lies more than 100 miles away from the United States boundary, that part of the country upon which our economy must more and more depend.
Then I come to an example of the difficulty of geological survey work. I think I will read part of this report to the committee because it gives some idea of the tremendous job the geological survey are attempting to

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys do and are doing in Canada. It is at page 19 and concerns the development in British Columbia. It states:
On account of the rugged terrain and accessibility factors, geological mapping of a standard Cordilleran map sheet bounded by two degrees of longitude and one degree latitude, requires a minimum of four years, which is twice the time ordinarily required for an equal area in other regions of Canada.
Not only does it require more time; it requires different equipment and more machinery and devices which have been developed by the scientists of the department.
The challenge that faces us is so tremendous that it staggers the imagination. I will just give one or two examples. I cite the metals tantalum and columbium which are essential in modern industry and which up to now have been available only in Nigeria, Brazil and the Belgian Congo. Five geologists detailed to do investigation work in the Yellowknife and Great Slave areas conducted detailed investigations at Great Slave lake; and there is a possibility that, through the work of these five geologists, this continent may become self-sufficient in those important metals. Then there is the discovery of a deposit of base metals at Campbell Chibougamau which has recently come into such prominence. That is another example of the work that is being done.
I do not propose to go further into this matter of our geology, Mr. Chairman. I do not propose to deal, except briefly, with the job that is being done in the mine dressing laboratories. The difficulty about the huge variety of different types of ore which have been developed in Canada is that they are useless unless a method of extraction can be developed and made commercially profitable. The ore dressing laboratories have done a splendid job in this regard. We who benefit by the economy of Canada owe to these scientists a debt which I think is greater than we at the present time realize.
I want to say, however, that there is one warning which should be heeded, and I think the minister brought it out when he spoke. These men who are doing this work, particularly the work of the geological survey, are making reports of a scientific nature. When those reports are completed they are of the utmost value to all the people of Canada. But those reports are the responsibility of the geologists, surveyors and technical men who prepare them. Under no circumstances should they be released until the technical men in charge have finished with them. There should be no such thing as prior information. I have seen these parties working. They say, "We hope we do not discover an ore body." I think they have
fMr. Adamson.]

been extremely accurate and ethical in the way they have presented their reports. But there is the danger that these reports receive publicity before they are finalized. I think that is one of the difficulties and one of the dangers we must guard against, in view of the tremendous amount of work that is being done at the present time.
If there is any criticism of this department, it is this. I feel that the $1,300,000 extra expenditure under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act should not be an expense against the department. That is an expense directly caused by the policy of the Department of Finance. The increase in salaries I agree with; but I should have liked to see that $1,300,000 expended on more surveys, on more geophysical work, on magnetometer work and on the discovery of more anomalies and new techniques throughout the country. As I tried to say when I began, the rate of development in Canada today absolutely defies description. It offers a challenge that no other people have ever faced, and the work cannot proceed fast enough. We are on the threshold. If we have the wisdom, if we have the political ability not to destroy the heritage which is offered to us, we can become one of the great powers because of our heritage of natural resources and particularly because of our heritage of mineral resources for which this department is responsible. I only hope we can accept that challenge and be prepared really to develop the country as the picture is just unfolding before us.

Later a final

coloured plan and final report are also made available to the prospectors, to the mining companies and to all those who are interested in looking for new mineral discoveries. Prior to two years ago, in our district those maps and reports were made available to the prospectors through the offices of the various mining recorders, and they were distributed free of charge.
Since that time a prospector who wishes to have a map has to fill out a card and send it to the department. If the prospector is not in a hurry that is all right, but if the prospector wants the map in a hurry, then I think it is a big disadvantage to have to send to Ottawa to get it. I would suggest that the minister consider very seriously the possibility of going back to the old system of having those maps available in the offices of the mining recorders in all the provinces.
We have good reason to ask for that, and I shall cite only one example. Three years ago a very important discovery was made not far from Amos in the constituency of Chapleau. That discovery today is the Bar-vue mine. This mine will be in production within the next month or two. When the discovery was made the prospectors were interested in staking some ground surrounding that discovery. In order to make their staking as profitable or as practical as possible they naturally wanted to get some information on the geology of the district. The only way for them to get that information was to secure a map which would show the geology. If they had had to write to Ottawa to get the maps it would have taken probably four or five days or maybe a week, and by the time they received the map there would have been no ground available in the surrounding district, because a week after the discovery the whole of one township was staked and more. Therefore I would suggest to the minister that we go back to the old system, even if the department has to charge a nominal sum for those maps. I think we would render a great service to the prospectors by making these maps available through the mining recorders in the different districts.
The work being done by the geological survey branch of this department is really No. 1 work, and I wish to congratulate those who are associated with it. Many reports and maps are being published, and I see no reason why those maps and reports should not be made available to those who are really interested in them. Moreover I think it is the aim of the department to do everything it can to encourage the development of our natural resources. I am sure that if

I know the minister does not want to hear long speeches, and most of the members do not want to make long speeches at the present time. Everybody is tired of talking and of listening, but I have a few remarks I want to make on the estimates of this department. This is one department that it seems to me has been somewhat neglected in the past as far as discussion in the house is concerned. The estimates always went through very quietly; but new activities are being undertaken by this department as well as by others; we are becoming better acquainted with them, more services are demanded, and so forth.
When he opened the discussion of his estimates the minister stated there never was a time in the history of Canada when there was a greater search for or a greater need of minerals than at the present time. I agree with that statement. He made reference to the few observations I had made in the debate on the amendment of the leader of the opposition which dealt with the question of international markets. I am not going to go into what I said in any great detail, except to say that the action of the department in respect of my request was anything but satisfactory.
The minister has said that it was a request from a private company. It was not a request from a private company. The fact of the matter is that the people who made the request were prospectors. They had all of their analyses made and the property was practically proven; but the capital available to form the company could not be obtained until the magnetic survey was completed. That was what was required by those who had the money and were quite willing to put it into the property. But the person who had the lease on the property at the time, and who over a period of some four years did the prospecting, unfortunately died within the last month. His wife still resides in North Sydney. I do not know whether or not she is interested in going forward with the project.
The person in question, Mr. H. W. Taylor, was a prospector who had spent about four years of his time in prospecting the area. He had leased some 57 square miles from the provincial government, and was in touch with an English company that had taken some of the samples. They had agreed that if the property was developed there was a market in England for about a million tons of the ore per year.

I sent all the correspondence to the minister's office, and I was disappointed to learn that the survey could not be made in Nova Scotia. They did not have the necessary equipment. In view of the search for minerals now going on, and the amount of time this man and his wife had put into proving the property, I felt it was not unreasonable to ask the department to use the equipment they have to complete the survey, always having in view the possibility of developing another industry in the maritime provinces, particularly when industries are so badly needed there.
The answer I received was that surveys of that kind were not undertaken for private companies. Perhaps I would be prepared to agree with that proposition. But this was a company in the embryo stage. The survey was necessary in order to enlist capital in the company. Had that been done I am sure the rest would have followed automatically. I was disappointed by the position taken by the minister because, in reality, these two people were prospectors who had a good chance to form a prosperous company, if the survey had taken place.
It did not take place, and I would hope that the department might take a further look into the matter. I can well understand that it cannot send this type of equipment all over the country at the request of any little company that thinks it may have a prospect. That would not be reasonable. On the other hand I believe there should be enough flexibility in the administration of the department to take a look at that kind of proposition, particularly where there are extenuating circumstances involving two people of this kind who spent four years in prospecting. According to the letters and other data I have seen this was a pretty good prospect. Nevertheless, at some time in the future some other, bigger company may undertake the work.
While I am critical on this particular point, let me say that I have had pleasant experiences in dealing with another section of the minister's department. I refer to that section in which chemical analyses of minerals are made. I have had a good deal of this work done in that branch of the department, and I have always found it courteous and efficient. I would refer particularly to Mr. J. A. Fournier with whom I had the pleasure of doing business. There is no difficulty in getting the work done when it comes within the scope of that particular branch of the department.
The fact remains, however, that in respect of this survey matter I was somewhat critical. I think a mistake was made, and that it
[Mr. Gillis.l
might well be corrected the next time we have to go at this sort of thing. We learn from our mistakes. I believe we lost a company there through not making the survey available when it was required. That is all I have to say on that score.
My main reason for speaking this evening is that I am still interested in the Nova Scotia coal industry, and there are one or two things I would like to say about it. First of all, I was disappointed in a recent appointment made to the board. That was the appointment of another coal operator. I have nothing against the appointee, except that he is a coal operator. This board was recommended by the Carroll commission following its survey of the coal industry in Canada. The recommendation to establish the coal board was contained in the minority report of the commission, written by Mr. A. J. Morrison, whom the minister knows well and who comes from Alberta.
Had it not been for the unions which had pressed for the commission in order to iron out the difficulties of marketing and the future development of coal, there would not have been a coal board. The case for the board was made by the unions, and the recommendation for its establishment came from the secretary-treasurer of the miners' unions in Alberta.
For that reason I say those who dig the coal are entitled to representation on the board. When it was set up I complimented the government, and pointed out I thought it was a move in the right direction. It would result in a central body having administration over subventions, regulations, marketing and all that sort of thing. I thought it was bringing skilled organization into the field and would bring sanity to the coal industry, because it was in a pretty haphazard condition from province to province.
Well, the board was set up. When it was established the late D. W. Morrison was appointed as the representative of labour. The other members on the board were either coal operators or coal importers. We went along with that without making much protest. My view always was that it should have been divided fifty-fifty as between operators and those who dig the coal, with an independent government chairman to act as referee.
Instead of having equal representation on the board, when Mr. Morrison, the labour representative, passed away another coal operator was appointed in his place. In my opinion it is a coal board no longer; it is now a coal operators' protective association, and can be used for that purpose. The interests

of most people and most organizations are selfish; and it is only natural to expect that the coal operator on the board will be thinking of his own interests. But another person is interested, and he is the man who digs the coal. In my view he is entitled to at least some representation. I hope the minister will rectify that mistake when he gets a chance, because it is a mistake.
The man who digs the coal had some respect for that board. I never heard much criticism of it. It was always thought to be doing a good job. Now we know something about subventions, where they are going and what amount is being paid. But their representative was taken off the board and replaced by another coal operator. The picture has changed and there is a lot of resentment. It may be a small thing to the minister or the department, but it is a big thing to the man who digs coal in Alberta, in British Columbia or in Nova Scotia. He feels that the one man who could speak for him on that board was removed and replaced by a coal operator. Perhaps the minister could be excused because he has only recently taken over the department. Perhaps the minister has never rubbed shoulders with that kind of thing and does not realize the psychological damage that was done to the coal miner when the labour representative on the board was removed.
The last annual report of the department indicates that considerable attention is being paid to research and that sort of thing in connection with the coal industry. Plans are being made to find other uses for coal. However, as far the the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is concerned, there does not seem to be much co-ordination between it and the users of coal, the Canadian National Railways, for example. The estimates indicate that $120,000 is being provided to McGill university for the purpose of developing a coal-fired turbine engine, and according to the departmental report this experiment is expected to be finished by the end of this year at which time we may have some idea what value there may be in such an engine.
Instead of the Canadian National Railways waiting to see what was going to be developed, Mr. Gordon told the committee a few weeks ago that they had a program for the complete dieselization of the Canadian National Railways-that is to use oil-which it is expected to be completed in the next five years. He stated that no more steam locomotives are being manufactured in North America, but that is not true. I have had some correspondence recently with a fairly large United States company which claims
19, 1952
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys that it is putting out a good type of coal-fired engine which compares favourably with the diesel.
What I am complaining about is that this government agency is rushing ahead as fast as it can to stop using coal on the Canadian National Railways. At the same time the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys are carrying on research to see if an engine using coal cannot be developed to operate just as efficiently and economically as a diesel engine. I think Mr. Gordon could well have carried on his program from Toronto west to a certain point and then gone rather slowly with dieselization east of Montreal.
The coal industry is most important to that part of the country, particularly to Nova Scotia. The C.N.R. market is around 288,000 tons per annum, but according to Mr. Gordon, at the end of five years that market will be pretty well wiped out. As I say, that is the main market for Nova Scotia coal.
Then we must consider natural gas. The government is granting a franchise to a company to pipe Alberta gas to Montreal and Quebec city. That gas will replace coal, not only for domestic purposes but for metallurgical purposes as well, because natural gas can be used in place of coal in any industry except basic steel. All these developments are taking place with the sanction of the government. At the same time the government is carrying on research to perpetuate the coal industry and make it more efficient. They are-putting $7,500,000 into a mechanization program for Dominion Steel and Coal. However, there is no over-all planning as far as the industry is concerned. One department seems to be working at cross purposes with the other instead of all these different people sitting down with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to see what can be done. In my opinion there is considerable evidence that there is no co-ordination of thinking in connection with this matter which is so vital to the economy of the country.
It is time the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys asked his colleagues in the government for a little more co-operation. I think this department is trying to do a good job in connection with this industry. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a pretty long-headed person and I remember back in 1947 he warned the coal operators of this country that if they did not watch themselves, develop their industry, conserve resources, and bring in new techniques, in a few years they might be faced with the kind of thing the coal operators of Great Britain were faced with at that time. I think that is quite true.
Despite all these developments in gas, oil and all that kind of thing, I think we must

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys realize that for a long time to come there will be a definite place for coal in the economy of North America. I think the minister should ask his colleagues whether there is any future for the coal industry in Nova Scotia. The government has a $10 million investment in the industry in the maritimes which has been made only recently. The government is helping to mechanize the industry, but what is its future? Is Mr. Gordon right in rushing ahead to dieselize the whole system? The economy of this province is being threatened, and at the same time the government is carrying on research on a turbine engine which may be more efficient and economical than the diesel. Is Mr. Gordon in too much of a hurry? What effect will natural gas have when it comes down from Alberta?
I am not against progress, but I do not think it is good sense to destroy the economy of one section of the country in order to make the cost of fuel a little less in another section. We have talked to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour about it. After reading this report and looking at these estimates it is evident that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is actually coming into its own. These matters have never been treated before as a mining proposition; everything else was dealt with, but not that. Today we have geological operations, research, subventions; all these matters are concentrated in the department. For the first time it is really getting down to business and doing a decent job.
What the minister must do is tell the other departments that they should not work at cross purposes with his. They should all sit down with the coal board and study this whole proposition before they start handing out money for pipe lines and all that kind of thing to offset the work this department is doing. While I am critical of the amount of co-operation we got in connection with the magnetic survey, from my reading of this report-I always read them-I think the department is doing the best job that has ever been done. I believe more members should take an active interest in the department and push it along a little. I do not think there is progress unless we have a little fight once in a while. That is the way we learn, and we keep people on their toes. I am quite satisfied with what the department is trying to do as far as the mining industry is concerned, but I am not satisfied with what a lot of other departments are doing to offset the work of this department. I will leave that to you. We are endeavouring to keep a fair balance between all these rival interests in our department. Perhaps it is a little difficult at times, but we are putting forth quite an effort to find new uses for coal and better methods of preparation. I have quite a lengthy statement here on the work of the fuels division, especially in relation to the coal mining industry. 1 think perhaps it would be worth while putting it on the record.
Projects having a direct bearing on the coal industry have pertained mainly to research on underground mine pressures and to coal preparation methods at collieries. This twofold investigation has been and is being conducted both in western and eastern Canada with the objective of studying the economic mining of coal at depth, with special attention to the avoidance of violent pressure "bumps" and "gas outbursts", in order to allow the safe mining of coal at greater depths than is now feasible; and to work with coal mining operators in helping them to clean and improve the quality of their product for the market. Special attention has been paid to the utilization of the finer sizes of bituminous coal which predominate in Canadian mining operations. A dozen mining engineers are now conducting field work in close association with the operators in Alberta, British Columbia, and Nova Scotia.
During the past decade a systematic study of the physical and chemical characteristics of Canadian coals as mined has been carried out. To date the coals mined at 150 different collieries have been investigated, which means that the properties of coals from practically all the larger producing mines have been studied and the results reported. This investigation affords information of great value to the operators in sizing and cleaning their product for various uses.
Other projects of a minor nature of direct assistance to the coal mining industry are the analyses of mine air gases and tests on the inflammability of coal mine dusts. These are concerned mainly with mine safety measures. The publication of the Canadian coal analyses, and co-operation with purchasing agents of government departments in their coal purchases according to quality specifications, has been continued during recent years.
Long term projects, with the increased use of Canadian coals in view, pertain to its use
3462	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys in a coal-fired gas turbine unit and to producing synthetic liquid fuels by hydrogenation. The objective of the first is to develop a coal-fired gas turbine primarily for locomotive use. If such a prime mover can be produced it will benefit the coal mining industry by retaining part of the coal market that will otherwise be lost to diesel or other types of oil-fired locomotives. The railways will also benefit because coal is generally the cheapest fuel on the basis of heating value.
The general purpose of the hydrogenation project is to investigate and improve upon partly developed methods for converting coal and heavy petroleum oil crudes to high grade liquid fuels. The Canadian reserve of petroleum, which is fast approaching the country's peacetime requirements, would not satisfy the demand if petroleum from the Middle East and South America were drastically restricted under wartime conditions.
Domestic stoker coal and coking investigations should also be mentioned. The increased use of Canadian coal in domestic stokers is under constant study. Installation of an experimental testing unit has been completed, and a series of tests has begun to compare the value of Canadian coals with standard imported coals; and the results are expected to be of assistance to manufacturers of equipment in improving stoker design.
Experiments were recently conducted on the blending of western bituminous coals, particularly from the Crowsnest area, to aid in promoting the increased and more efficient use of Canadian coals for making coke for foundry and other metallurgical uses. With the object of materially improving the physical properties of metallurgical coke for use in blast furnaces at steel plants in the east, the blending of Nova Scotia coals varying considerably in volatile matter content is also being intensely investigated.
In co-operation with the dominion coal board the division of fuels has recently completed a survey of the industrial market for Canadian coals. It has been concluded that there is a market for approximately one million additional tons of these coals a year, provided the coals meet minimum requirements in regard to cost and delivery.

speechtext:
After listening to the remarks of the leader of the opposition with reference to this department I am going to make a few observations, because I feel that perhaps I have a little background in connection with this department.
I was the first minister when the department was organized. I will admit that I was perhaps a little sceptical, too, as the leader of the opposition is, that there might be duplication of services as between the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the various departments of mines of the different provinces. After a rather thorough examination I was convinced that such condition did not actually exist.
If one goes over the history of the old department of mines and resources he will find that mines was one particular branch of it. I can give the committee illustrations to indicate the great advantage that has been enjoyed by this country in the development of its natural resources because of the fact that the mines branch existed.

Before me here this evening is the director of scientific services who as a young man, twenty-five or thirty years ago, was out in the province of Alberta on geological surveys for a number of years, and to him and to his staff more than to any other group of people in this Dominion of Canada may be credited today the wonderful development that is going on at this time in the Alberta oil fields. Had it not been for the fact that geological surveys were made in that province thirty years ago and the mapping was done, there would not be the development there is today in the province of Alberta.
The function of the department lies in finding out where these resources are, in presenting maps that geologists and prospectors may use. I will give a typical example, which is a true one. Years and years ago in the Eldorado district where the present great deposit of uranium is in this country, maps were made and it was indicated, and it was on the records here in Ottawa, that there was a deposit of uranium in that country. Gilbert La Bine, who organized the Eldorado Mining Company as a result of that map, went into that country and found and developed one of the greatest resources we have in Canada today, a resource which was taken over by the government of this country at a time when it was very urgently needed.
The function that has been carried out for years is for the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to make these geological and geodetic surveys, to prepare the maps which are freely available to any citizen of this country who is interested in the development of the mining resources.
The function of the provincial people is mostly in the line of development. These resources belong to the provinces. They have been developed by the provinces. In the province of Ontario the great development that took place in the Cobalt country, in Kirkland lake and in the Porcupine; the development in northwestern Quebec, where hundreds of millions of dollars have come into the coffers of the people of this country, have been the result of the initial surveys and developments of the department of mines of the federal government.
Do you know what the mineral wealth of this country is at the present time? Last year $1,200 million of new wealth was taken out of the ground in Canada. That is growing yearly, and the time is not far distant when wealth to the value of $2 billion will be developed from the mining and oil industry of Canada. I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that the money spent by this department is well spent. True the costs of administration may have gone up. They have gone up in

Because of increased wages, because of the fact that all the materials which are being used have increased in price, because of the increases in staff and in highly paid technical people who are necessary in order to carry on this work. For instance, take the hydrographic surveys. We are mapping the seas of this country, mapping out where the fishing areas are; and in times of war or potential war these hydrographic surveys are of great benefit to this country for our own protection. It is costly to maintain ships, as they do in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys; therefore costs must necessarily go up.
Without speaking at any greater length, Mr. Chairman, I must say I cannot agree with the leader of the opposition. I feel that perhaps he is not as well informed as he might be with reference to the function of the various departments provincially and federally. But the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys federally are doing the fundamental work, the a, b, c work, with reference to the development of the resources of Canada, and in the main the provinces are reaping the benefit.

The fact is that the development of mining in this country has been remarkable and a challenging story of development. Nothing that I have said in any way changes that. In fact what I have said on numerous occasions in this house and elsewhere is that there is no more challenging story in Canada than the story of mineral discovery, very largely related to the information which has been made available through the various departments in regard to mineral possibilities. I would ask the minister, however, simply so that a very remarkable story shall not be confused, to check back on his story about Gilbert La Bine, because it was an even more remarkable story than he has indicated. It was remarkable because of the fact that there was no accurate map at the time he made the discovery. The maps we now have which show the location of the Eldorado mine are, as a matter of fact, the result of the work done under another estimate which will appear later, which provides for the photographing of the great territories of this country where other kinds of mapping may not have taken place.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

It was indicated long before that, because Gilbert La Bine told me himself.

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Yes, it was indicated in 1780, which was long before this government came to power, and it was actually on a map drawn by Hearne at the time he made a trip down from Coppermine through that area. I am not saying this facetiously. I am saying it because I believe it is one of the most remarkable and challenging stories in our mineral history. Samuel Hearne recorded seeing evidence of mineral outcroppings at what later turned out to be the very point where Gilbert La Bine discovered what became the Eldorado mine.
I am not raising this by way of criticism.
I am only saying that it is a fantastic story, and that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys itself can claim great credit for the fact that after discovery was made, through co-operation with the air services very accurate maps of that whole tremendous mineral area were prepared by air photography. What I do want to emphasize is this. No one is more convinced than I of the immense possibilities of mineral development in this country. This department has been doing excellent work for many years, before there were departments of mines in some of the provinces and in fact before some of those provinces had established claim to these resources. This department is doing excellent work today. Throughout the years the men who have served the department have established a name for devotion to service, and highly efficient service, that is recognized throughout the world. No one would be more anxious than I to make sure their services are recognized. I am not talking about the efforts made by individuals; I am not talking about individual devotion to service; I am not talking about the great achievements of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I am simply suggesting that in this huge business of government under a federal system, where departments are occupying the same fields, in the light of the excellent things that are being done, and of the increased responsibility, there should be an attempt to save money where money can be saved. I suggest that an effort be made to get the departments together and examine xhe possibility of co-ordinating their activities in a manner that will make it possible to perform their service on the most economical basis.

Earlier this session, Mr. Chairman, I directed certain remarks of mine to the coal industry, particularly as it applies to my province; and after all Alberta is that Canadian province in which the greater amount of coal is produced. It also represents the area in which we have the greatest known reserves. I just happen to represent a constituency in which coal mining is an important industry.
When I raised this question earlier I emphasized two important facts. First, I am inclined to believe that today the Canadian coal mining industry is deteriorating. I think all the evidence one is able to gather indicates that this is a fact. In the second place I emphasized the fact that should a war break out and our oil supplies in the Middle East be cut off, as I am afraid they would be, we would find ourselves calling upon the coal industry for substantial assistance just as we did during the last war. I am very much afraid, Mr. Chairman, if this condition of deterioration continues, and war does break out, we are going to call upon that industry to do what I am afraid it will be utterly incapable of doing. Once our coal mines are permitted to deteriorate to the point where they close and the workers are dispersed in other industries in Canada, then it becomes a problem of the first magnitude to get those mines back into operation.
I have gathered a few figures, but before I refer to those may I say to the minister that I am particularly pleased to learn that the closest co-operation exists between the minister of mines in Alberta, Mr. Tanner, and the coal board with respect to laying down quality regulations, as well as the stamping of coal that does attain a certain quality in order that we may be assured of our best quality coal being shipped into central Canada. The minister indicated that while there has been no change in the subvention, it still represents an amount which enables us to put Alberta coal into central Canada-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member is misinformed. The subvention rate was increased last year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I am sorry, but I understood the minister to say there had been no change. Even so, I would remind the minister of the freight increases which have taken place during the last year-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

-which must have an effect upon the position of our Alberta coal in relation to coal which is marketed in central Canada.
In 1948 the Alberta industry produced
8,110,000	tons of coal. There was an increase in 1949 to 8,616,983 tons. We find a very sharp decline in 1950 to 8,138,206 tons, and a further substantial decline in 1951 to 7,661,276 tons. I fully realize that this decline in coal production in Alberta has been coincidental with, and one might even say attributable to, the increase in competition from laboursaving fuels, marketing difficulties due to freight rate increases and so on over the past several years. I do not believe there is any argument either about the obvious advantages of labour-saving, clean fuel; advantages which have enabled natural gas, for example, to supplant coal as a domestic and industrial fuel in most of our urban areas and larger towns in western Canada, particularly in my own province of Alberta.
Increasing competition has been felt, so the mine operators say, from liquid petroleum gases such as propane and butane, and from fuel oil in some rural areas. One of the things that does concern me is this.
During the past number of years the railways have represented our most substantial consumer of coal. According to figures which I have, in 1948 the railways consumed 2,312,273 tons of Alberta coal. In 1949 it went up to 3,126,425 tons; in 1950 to 3,308,365 tons. Then there was a sharp decline in 1951 to 2,443,326 tons. The railways which in the past have provided the largest non-seasonal market for Alberta coal are proceeding with a plan which will ultimately result in the conversion to diesel power of both of our transcontinental system. In the meantime an increasingly large number of steam locomotives are using fuel oil rather than coal. This oil, of course, is obtained as a by-product of light fuel production at refineries using light crude stock or from the particular heavy crude fuels such as those we find in Lloyd-minster, Vermilion and Wainwright. This railway conversion program apparently completely ignores the possibility that in the case of war or in case of any national emergency there may be an acute oil shortage, as I have already stated, and in the meantime some of our mines may have had to close down with the resultant dispersal of trained

personnel. I think that is a matter to which the railways themselves should give serious consideration.
I have already mentioned the competition from other forms of fuel. While facing that unabated competition from other types of fuel, coal mine operators have had to contend with constantly increasing marketing costs brought on, I would say, in the main by freight rate increases over the past several years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: And production costs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

And production costs. The increased production costs resulting in substantial part from heavier shipping costs brought about by freight rate increases have meant substantially increased overhead costs, thus placing the mines in an extremely inferior marketing position. Each increase in freight rates has further restricted markets when the industry is in no position to absorb these extra costs. If one examines the facts of the case I think he will find that every time we have had a freight rate increase in Canada we have lost markets for Alberta coal. They were simply put in this difficult position where they could not compete at all with imported coals.
To meet this situation which threatens death by strangulation if a large increase in production should be requested-such as, I might emphasize, was obtained by the federal government during the last war-efforts are being made to prepare more marketable products from coal. I think that is probably one of the healthy signs. I am going to ask the minister a few questions with respect to that matter. When I say that the industry is threatened by strangulation, I think I am not stating anything that is foreign to the facts which exist at the present time. I know it can be said that the number of mines in operation in Alberta, for example, has increased since 1948 from 94 to 104 in the case of subsurface mines. There has been a decrease in strip mine operations during the same period of time. But while there has been an actual increase in the number of subsurface mines operating between 1948 and 1951, I think the facts are that most of the increase in mining operations is represented in the smaller mines or the family mines, as we know them. The significant fact, of course, is that during those four years we have had an important decline in actual coal production.
I realize fully that certain efforts are being made to produce other products from coal in my province. As I said a moment ago, in that connection I think I see a hopeful sign. I have noticed that they are concentrating more and more upon the manufacture
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys of briquettes. That procedure is going on in the Coalspur, Mountain Park, the Crows-nest pass, Canmore and Seebe areas in Alberta. Coke is also processed in Coleman. I am told that greater attention is being given to the manufacture of coke and briquettes. There seems to be a rather satisfactory market for those products.
I am going to ask the minister if he has any information with respect to "fabricoal". I am not too certain what it is. I know that at Big Valley, Alberta, activity has been under way for some time, and I understand that about 1,742 tons of that product were marketed outside of the province last year. As I say, I do not know exactly what "fabricoal" is but I am particularly interested in it. If it represents an activity that might provide further marketing opportunities for Alberta coal, it is of course natural that we are all for it. I should like to have the minister comment upon that matter, if he will, when I am finished.
I should like to stress the point that the thing I fear above all else is deterioration in the coal mining industry to or beyond the point where we may find it utterly impossible to rehabilitate that industry in time of great emergency. I know that certain changes are conceivably inevitable. I realize fully, of course, that if one has an opportunity to burn gas, he is not likely to burn coal when it represents a product that is dirtier to handle, shall we say, and which, through the process of combustion, produces ashes which have to be removed.
I also appreciate that it may be quite natural for the railroads to move from coal burners to oil burners. But I think the one thing the railroads should realize is that this may not be the proper time to do that. If the international picture were somewhat different from the one we see at the present time, then I would say: "Surely; move along in unrestricted fashion in this process of conversion." But I am a bit fearful. I am not talking for a handful of coal miners who may be in my constituency because I realize that it is quite possible, without too much difficulty, to rehabilitate coal miners and move them into other industries. But I know you cannot move them back as easily as you can move them out. In the light of the international situation I am fearful that we may not be doing all we can to keep this industry in a healthy state in order to meet any emergency that might develop.
I wish the minister would go into this question of subventions a little more fully. Have subvention increases kept pace with increased transportation costs? Can he give us some further information with respect to

When I was first elected I tried, in my small way, to study the coal mining industry, and I decided to make a speech about it each year. Evidently, however, my speeches were not very powerful, because it appears I cannot get very much action from the government in respect of any over-all national coal policy.
Perhaps as the years have passed I have weakened a little in my efforts. I carried on a sort of annual speech-making event on behalf of the coal mining industry. This is my seventeenth year in the House of Commons and I do not propose to repeat my speech this year, because I do not expect it would bring any better results than it has in the past.
The picture is a dismal one. In the past years I have seen no change in the government's attitude toward the coal mining industry, and toward bringing into existence a coal mining policy that would give some hope to what would now appear to be a dying industry. Yet nothing seems to have changed. The coal is the same kind of coal we have mined for years; the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway are just the same; they still run their trains on the same tracks. Although there may have been some changes in methods and equipment, the coal mines are the same and the consumers are the same. We have industries as well as domestic consumers in Canada. The unfortunate thing is that the government is the same. We have had the same government for a number of years. All this adds up to one thing, and that is that the coal situation is just the same and it does not look as though there will be much improvement in the future.

There was quite a flurry a few years ago when the Carroll coal commission travelled across the country and spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in its efforts. It was quite a show, and it gave some hope to the coal mining industry while the sittings were going on in various places. A lengthy report was published, and a good deal of valuable information appeared in it. The commission was well manned, and had on it a representative of labour as well as one from industry. In short the commission was well rounded. The report was voluminous and valuable; but what happened to it? No recommendations were adopted. It has now been filed away on some musty old shelves in government offices, and the only real use to which it has been put, evidently, is to make fodder for mice and other starving rodents.
That is the situation. The coal mining industry is concerned with the advent of the diesel engine. As the minister is aware, most of the coal mined in Alberta for industrial purposes is for use on the railroads. The diesel engine is upsetting the calculations of the coal mining industry. I would ask the minister to tell us the government's policy to keep this industry on its feet.
Referring to an earlier vote the minister said that a market for about a million tons of coal was now available. I was disappointed when he did not tell us where that market is. Evidently it is a new one somewhere, and I would ask him to tell us where it is, because a million tons would make a worth-while addition to what we already have.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I do not agree with the hon. member when he refers to coal mining as a dying industry, any more than I would agree to gold mining being described as a dying industry. Coal mining is fundamental to


our industrial life. I believe, so far as Canada is concerned, that when the gas and oil that has captured the imagination of the public at the present time, and for very good reason, has been used up, coal will be very important. It does any industry good to have a little squeeze once in a while, and I think the coal industry is no exception. They will have to improve their methods if they wish to survive. That process may be a little painful, but I believe it will survive.
The dominion coal board was created to do and is now doing everything possible to assist the industry through this period of transition. Through advertising the coal board does everything possible to promote the use of Canadian coal in Canada. We do not advertise Alberta coal specifically, but we direct our efforts toward benefiting the coal industry of Canada generally.
I believe the Alberta government, with which my hon. friend is very friendly, has definite responsibilities in respect of Alberta coal. The gas and oil development which is contributing to the prosperity of Alberta and of the Alberta government especially is doing more than diesels to put the coal industry of Alberta out of business. Therefore I feel that the Alberta government has a direct responsibility to the coal industry.
Recently the Alberta government allocated a certain amount of gas for export to the Pacific coast. That will affect a very important market for Alberta coal and will create a further problem for the coal industry of that province. I believe the Alberta government will measure up to its responsibility because it has been most co-operative so far. I certainly hope they will go much further.
If my hon. friend would like to know what has happened as a result of the reports of royal commissions on the coal industry and so on, I suggest that' he read our annual report.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: The minister referred to a million tons.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: The report I put on the record was made by the fuels branch of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. That market is wherever it can meet competition. There is a market anywhere in Ontario for Alberta coal if it can meet competition.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
If that is the answer, why limit it to one million tons, why not five million or ten million tons? The minister mentioned specifically that there was a market for one million tons. That was the figure he read from the document and I would like to know where it is. So far we have had no answer. It is like a dog chasing his

own tail, it just gets nowhere. However, if that is the minister's answer I shall not press it, as I understand we want to get on with the items tonight.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: The present transportation facilities from western Canada would limit the movement of coal to Ontario to not more than half a million tons per year. At the present time there is a competitive market for an additional three-quarters of a million tons of Canadian coal in Quebec. That would make more than a million tons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Is the mechanization of the maritime coal industry making satisfactory progress? I notice the production is down this year as compared with last.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: The progress to date of the mechanization program is not satisfactory either to the dominion coal board or to the operators. Many difficulties have been encountered, largely due to the defence program. They have been unable to get certain types of electrical equipment. They are changing from a compressed air to an electrical operation, and it has been difficult to make the hoped-for progress. We are keeping closely in touch with it. One engineer from the department went there a few weeks ago, and we are sending two more in the fall of the year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Is the department trying to work out new methods of using Alberta coal for the manufacture of chemicals and other things?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: New equipment is being installed at the moment in the Booth street laboratory for the hydrogenation of coal and other heavy fuels. In this connection they deal with very high pressures.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: That is turning it into liquid?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: We are experimenting with turning it into liquid, and also trying to develop new combustion methods.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Under normal circumstances we would pursue certain matters a little further, but due to the lateness of the hour and I am sure the anxiety of the minister to get his estimates through, in co-operation with the committee, so we can get on to external affairs tomorrow, we will forgo asking further questions. We have expressed our feelings to the minister and to the government, and no doubt when we next have a chance we will bring up this matter again.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys 247. Payments in connection with the movements of coal under conditions prescribed by the governor in council, $6,000,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I do not want to be cast in the role of a prophet, but I would not be at all surprised if some of the younger members now in the house will some day see coal being used mainly not as a fuel but in the production of synthetic materials in the petrochemical industry. What research is being done in developing by-products from coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Other than the hydrogenation project we have no specific undertakings at the present time. The men in the department keep in close touch with experiments being carried on in the United States. We do not undertake any experimental work that is being duplicated elsewhere in Canada or the United States where we have access to the results.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: This department is responsible for the production of probably $1,500 million worth of products which form the sinews of most of our manufacturing and which will become more and more important as the years go by. I suggest to the minister that at the next session the committee on mines, forests and waters be convened so that the experts of the department, the directors and others, may come and inform members as to what is being done. I think that is one of the essential jobs of the technical personnel in the department.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
